Now, if you are content to aceept the services of one who has not gone the whole length with you, it not only affords me plerisure, but I feel it a serious duty to help forward the temperance movement in every way that lies in my power. (Hear, hear.) At the same time, heel it woul•i be inconsistent in me to occupy I ,this chair without stating the fact that lam not a teetotaller. One of the strongest convictions on my mind is that the vitality, and consequently the pros- parity of this country are being sapped by this brutal. Icing vice of intemperance; but this is the smallest part of the mischief that is being produced by our dreadful drinking habits. Our prisons are being filled, thousands, yea, airiest millions of victims in our land, in no way responsible for the drunkenness of those who are degrading them, are brought to poverty and ruin; and this mighty barrier to all intellectual, moral, and religious growth is constantly on the in- crease. (Hear, hear.) I was much struck with a review of the quarterly revenue returns in the Daily News a few days since. You all know the depressed condition in whiah the business of this country has been for the last year or two, and in the face of re- ports that meet you in every newspaper from the manufacturing centres, you will find it hard to believe that the purchasing power of the country is increasing. These figures show that the revenue &lived from the duty on intoxicating drink is still largely on the ec... crease ; and the .Daily News takes comfort from this awful fact, and argues that the country is still mode- rately proeperods, and its purchasing power augment- ing, otherwise this increase would not have taken place. I venture to believe that anyone who has watched the course of the drunkard will come to a different conclusion. No barrier will be allowed to come in between him and the frightful craving of his appetite. Character, credit, wife, children, and every-. thing that makes life desirable, will be sacrificed to gratify this insatiable thirst. These figures, as well as thousands of other corroborating facts, prove to my mind that the drunkenness of this country is fright- fully on the increase, and I trust my teetotal friends will excuse me for sayin g that, while I ascribe all honour to them for their noble efforts, I cannot have strong faith in the result. It Is darting straws against the wind, and shooting Niagara, well meant, but utterly inadequate. If we talk of the Alliance movement, and invoke the aid of legislation, we are told we cannot reform men by act of Parliament. Certainly legisla- tion, by increasing the facilities for indulging in drink- ing habits, has done much to create drunkards; and I have frequently observed that those who are so scep- tical in regard to the potency of law, are not usually consistent. No sane man expects an act of Parlia- ment to change a man's heart, to convert a lion into a lamb, or to eraaicate vicious appetites; but if we con- demned all human law because it does not possess this attribute of God, a very little legislation would do us. (Hear, hear.) Laws against murder, robbery, violence, thefts, and other crimes do not make men good, pure, loving, and gentle; but few will be found to denounce them as interfeling with our liberty, or useless for the protection of society. because these are tasks beyond their power. It is rer lly useless to argue against such a positicn. and it is difficult to believe in the honesty ef those who use such phrases. We believe an act of Parliament, if honestly enforced, can prevent drunk- enness—(hear, hear)—and we ask and expect it to do no more; and as it gives peace, order, and protection to life and property, we believe it can compel the drunkard to become sober, that -it can smooth the pillow of many a broken hearted wife, and feed and clothe multitudes of children, who have never known anything but want and neglect. Yee, it can do more. It "an excite the gratitude of many a poor drunkard DOW groaning under a passion he is unable to resist, and crying in vain for the help that our Christian Country denies him. How many poor slaves of drink pray that they may never see another drop, because it Is irresistable as long as it is accessible. In conclusion, I wish to say that my only objection to the Alliance movement is, that it does not go far enough for me. I would give magistrates the right of closing public. houses, and I believe we would get such an act quite as soon as we shall obtain this power for two-thirds of the ratepayers-. (Cheers.) It may not come speedily. but present appearances indicate that the time will come when our country will be compelled to make men, lee, and women also, sober. by act of _Parliament, earth; and lim prepared to welcome any legislation that promises to accomplish this end—the-Permissive Bill if adequate—but the Maine Liquor Law, if that be the only means of rescuing the hundreds of thousands that annually sink into a premature and hopeless grave. (Loud cheers.)

Wow.= moved the first resolution, which was as follows "That this meeting rejoices at the many signs of growing sympathy with, and the re- cognized importance of the temperance movement, as evinced in the establishment of temperance societies in connection with the various Christian Churches of the land, the opening of cathedral churches, and large places of worship to the promulgation of the principles, the formation of Bands of Hope and other efforts; and tenders its hearty thanks to those clergymen and ministers who kindly aided this work by their efforts in the pulpits in the town yesterday." As an old teeto- taller he welcomed the various temperance organisa- tions. and said he was glad the re!igions bodies of the country were taking the matter up. They had had sermons preached in various places of worship on the previous day, and they thanked the gentlemen who had done this, and right nobly did some of them ape*; if the Christian ministers and deacons and leaders of their churches and chapels would look at the matter in its true light, and take their true stand, they might hope that the young people might become endued with their principles. Some of them had long believed that it was possible to make people sober by Act of Parlia- ment, and he believed it would come to that before long. It was their duty to lay hold of every means to attain the results they had in view, and he therefore very heartily proposed the resolution he had read. (Cheers.)

Dr. J. H. GOINALL, who was cordially received, said : I have great pleasure in seconding the resolu- tion proposed by Mr. "Winskill. The temperance question is one that has my heartfelt sympathy and support, and I rejoice with you that it is now &s- -eaming its proper character, and that the profession to which I belong is beginning to recognise the truth of the principles this society has long advocated, viz,, that alcohol is not essential either as a beverage or as an article of diet. (Cheers.) Reference is made in the resolution to the valuable medical testimony which, in my opinion, makes this great question not only a social and a political, but a medical ques- tion. (Hear, hear.) With your permission I will quote a few opinions of the leading and most accurate thinkers my profession has produced. Dr. Richardson lays—" That to escape the evils arising from alcohol, there is only cue perfect course, namely, to abstain altogether from alcohol. (Hear, hear.) No fear need be entertained of any physical or mental harm from such abstinence. Every good may be expected from it, (Hear, hear.) A man or woman who abstains is healthy and safe. A man or woman who indulges at all is unsafe. A man or woman who relies on alcohol for support is lost." (Cheers.) Dr. Parkes, F.R.S., and who for 15 years had the care of the national health of our soldiers, and whose opinion on ques- tions of hygiene the medical profession have unanimou=.ly placed in the highest rank for his whole life was ever actuated by the purest desire to discover the truth. In his recent work on the personal care of health which was passing through the press when its lamented author was called away from his - labours says " That an article of diet to be necessary to man in a state of health must do either er all of , three different things, it must warm him, nourish him, ' Or supply him with power. In other words it must contribute heat, food, or force to the human economy." And by the most careful experiments he proves that alcohol does none of these things, and Dr. Sidney Rin- ger, an authority on the uses and actions of medicines says "That the experiments are so comlete that they must be accepted as authoritative." Sir Henry Thompson says "That fermented liquor of any kind Is unnecessary as an article of diet. Let us put alco- holic liquor in its proper place, namely, amongst the so-called luxuries of life, not_ amongst its necessaries. Take them frankly as n luxury, one which must be paid for by some persons very lightly, by some at a high price, but always to be paid for." (Hear, hear.) With such testimony as this to ignore the importance of total abstinence is to out-Dizzy Disraeli in treating of Turkish atrocities. (Laughter.) I hold, therefore, it Is the duty of every• member of my profession that they should fully impress upon the peopie that if they take intoxicating liquors they do not take them for the sake of their health, but for the sake of the pleasure and enjoyment which is prematurely pro- duced by intoxicating drinks—ro do all in his power to contribute some influence in chao Rima the of moiety, but also by coming on this and similar ' "e plat- forms, and publicly advocating Total Abstinence. div.head: WARRINGTON OLAIIIANT.
div.p: A WARRINGTON OLAIIIANT.

Another claimant has recently returned from' Ans. trails, and claims property amounting to about £6,000. The gentleman in question is Mr. John Alderson, of Warrington, who, after a residence of twelve years in Melbourne, has returned to Lancashire to find that hie paternal estate has been sold by his guardians, he alleges, illegally. The estate was left originally by John Shaw, of Frodsham, who died 1803, and the claimant inherits it through his mother, who married John Alderson. His brother, Mr. Henry Alderson, glass manufacturer, of Warrington, was appointed one of the executors. Another executor was a Liver- pool ship broker, who, it is alleged when he heard that t .43 heir-at-law had sailed for Melbourne, was the means of selling the property on a chance title, and the present holder of the estate is a well-known and respected member of the Town Council and Board A 9nardians at Warrington. The gentlemen who acted as executors, &a., are now deceased, and the only gentleman living connected with tho dispute beside the claimant himself is the present holder of the estate. He contends that the property was purchased under thoroughly legal conditions by auction, and therefore he has nothing whatever to do with any imaginary claim which may be brought forth. However, legal action has already been taken in the matter, and the occupier and tenants of the estate been served with notices of ejectment. Mr. Alderson states that the person under whose will the estate was sold was at the time of his death insolvent; therefore it is con- tended he had not the power,to dispose of the property. A well-known baronet is also a member of the family interested, and the dispute is causing considerable in- terest in Warrington and neighbourhood. The case is expected to come on in one of the London courts next term, unless the venue is changed to Liverpool.

div.head: CONVICTION OF DR. SLADE, THE
div.p: THE CONVICTION OF DR. SLADE, THE
SPIRITITALIST.

"Dr." Slade, the Spiritualist "medium," was on Tuesday convicted under the Vagrant Act of a fraudulent imposture. The magistrate at Bow-street, Mr. Flowers, held that on the evidence it was impossible to doubt that Slade wrote the words which were found on the elate by Professor Lankester and Dr. Donkin. Consideling the grave mischief likely to result from such practices, the Magistrate felt that he could not mitigate the punishment imposed by the law, and therefore he sentenced Slade to be imprisoned for three months, with hard labour. Notice of appeal was given and, the defendant was liberated on bail. The appeal will be heard life the Middlesex magistrates at the session in the third week of January.

COAL—There is no very material change-generally to notice in the coal trade of this district, and prices for house coal remain much the same as last month. Oommon coal is not quite such a drug as it was, but the demand for this description of fuel is not at all brisk. There is rather a lessened production of burgy, and in the Manchester district advances of 6d. to 10d. per ton are being asked. slack is very plentiful in the market, especially the commoner sorts, and there is a weaker tone in prices. hog.—There is only a moderate demand for iron in the district, and the market during the past week has len rather dull. One or two brands of common iron which are offering in this district help to keep prices down, but the principal makers are very firm, at late rates. The position of Lancashire makers of pig iron shows no improvement, but that they remain, however, vary firm in their prices, and for delivery into the Manchester districts quotations still range about 655. to 575. per ton for No. 3 foundry, and 555. per ton for No. 4 forge. Middlesborough iron delivered here is quoted at 645. 9d. per ton for No. 3 foundry, 631. 9d. for No. 4 foundry, and 625. 3d. per ton for No. 4 forge. i In the finished iron trade there s not much change to notice; some of the large firms are well supplied with orders for the next two or three months, but in many cases works are only kept going from hand to mouth, and very few orders of any magnitude are at present being given out. THE WEATIM, TEE CROPS, AND TEE CORN TRADE. —The Mark-lane Express says—" Very little rain has fallen during the past week, and altogether consider- able improvement has taken place in the weather, though the days have been dull and cold. In the north the remains of long outstanding crops have been carted in, but in a most deplorable condition after continuous heavy rains. Barley and oats have suffered so severely in many districts of Scotland that it is questionable whether the grain is worth carting at all. 'Very gloomy reports are also afloat as to the potato crop. Though the disease is at present con- fined to a few districts in England and Scotland, it is much to be feared that the crop in Ireland is suffering severely. Great progress has been made with the sowing of wheat during the past week, especially in Norfolk and other wheat-growing districts. Political influences, which last week were the ruling power in the trade, have now assumed a less ominous aspect. The possibility of war, nevertheless, remains, and holders of wheat consequently maintain a fair attitude. Our local trade having been in a quiescent state, wheat has with difficulty maintained the advance caused by the recent excitement."

div.p: IMPORTANT CASE.
STARTLING CONFLICT OF EVIDENCE.

At the Altrincham Petty Sessions on Monday, before Mr. W. joynson (chairman), Messrs. J. Carlisle, and B. H. Joynson, William Etches, of George-street, Altrincham, was summoned for being drunk on Sun- day night, the 22nd October. Acting sergeant Harvey hated that shortly before ten o'clock on the night of the 22nd instant he saw the defendant, who staggered up the street into the Unicorn Hotel. As he went up the steps he fell against the side of the door, and went staggering along the lobby into the bar. He (Harvey) was standing opposite the door. The bar was lighted up with gas. It would be a quarter to ten. In the course of a coupls or three minutes, in company with P.C. Harrington, he went into the hotel. He found the defendant seated at a table with a glass of refresh. ment before him. The defendant, who was drunk, was in the act of pouring water into the glass. He was not positive what it was; it was whisky or brandy, a light yellow colour; it had very much the appearance of whisky. When the defendant was pouring the water, it both went in the glass and on to the table. He was so nervous or something, he could not pour the water into the glass. There were 14 or 16 persons in the bar, besides the landlord. Defendant.—What colour do you say P Harvey.—lt was a yellow colour. Defendant.—You cannot see very well ; it was white, It was Scotch whisky. P.C. Harrington said that he was in company with Hervey, and corroborated what be said. Mr. Stead.—That won't do, give the evidence. The Chairman.—He admits that be • had a glass of Scotch whisky. Defendant. —I was not fresh. I hal:only had three glasses that night. The Chairman.—Was he drunk P.C. Harrington.—He was *ivy drunk. If he had not held by the lamp post he would have fallenotud did fall against Yoniton's shop. Defendant.—l had had one glass at the Downs Hotel, another at Waterhouse% and the other at the Unicorn. As for stumbling, lain an old man. I was not drunk no more than I am now. The Chairman.—l perceive now the difficulty of having decided not to settle this case until the other against Harvey, the landlord, is heard. The charge of drunkenness on the premises is clearly brought before the Court. The defendant brings forward no evi- dence, but says the defence may be given in the other case. Mr. Stead (who appeared for Mr. Harvey).—That is the inconvenient mode of proceeding in the Court. You should have heard the other case first; that shows the inconvenience of the practice here, and it shows the reasonableness of the course adopted elsewhere. You may find him drunk on his„nwn testimony, and sober on that adduced afterwards. It is far more convenient to adopt the practice which is adopted elsewhere, and take the case of the innkeeper first. Superintendent Aston.—l apply for all the witnesses In the next case to be sent out of court. Mr. Stead.—Why did you. not apply before your Witnesses were beard. Mr. Aston.--The evidence against Harvey has not been heard. Mr. Stead.—lt is unfair that onel class of witnesses should be in and another out. Superintendent Aistsin—My witnesses were in and so were yours. It is no use your attempting to dictate to me, the bench will do that if necessary, I am in their hands. James Harvey, landlord of the "Unicorn" Hotel, Altrincham, was then charged with permitting drunkenness, to take place on his licensed premises, on Sunday night, the 22nd Oct. The Defendant.—l plead not guilty decidedly. - The witnesses were ordered out of court. Mr. Stead said that the only part of the evidence be objected to was that which referred to what took place between the officer and Mr. Etches, when the de- fendant was not present. Any statement that Etches made could not be taken as evidence against his Client. Active Sergeant Harvey stated that at a quarter to ten on Sunday night, the 22nd. inst., in company with P.C. Herrington he visited the " Unicorn" Hotel, Market-place, Altrincham. In the bar he found the defendant seated at a table with a glass of refreshment just supplied to him. Etches was drunk and witness drew the attention of the landlord to him. The defen- dant said, "Oh, I don't Arnow, I scarcely think he is drunk." Witness said, 'she is drunk, and has just come tumbling into the house, it is a very bad case, 'Sunday night, a man coming tumbling into your house, and you supplying him with refreshment. The Chairman.—Etches had drink before him. Witness.—Yes, and he was in the act of watering it. He witness saw Mr. Harvey on Thursday afternoon, when he said," Well, what about the case." Mr. Stead.—l object, you cannot prove your case by on admission made afterwards. Mr. Harris, the magistrates clerk.—You can. Witness.—l said its a bad case, it has been reported It will have to take its usual course. The defendant then said, "if the man was drunk you ought to have prevented him coming into the house." Witness said, "I have nothing to do with what he did in Victoria St. or with the control of your house." Superintendent.—Did you hear Etches when in the bar, make any remark ? Witness.—He said "I'm as drunk as a b— fool," that was when they, the officers were outside, and he Etches was in. That was before they entered. Mr. Harris.—Before or after he was supplied with drink. Witness.—Directly we hoard him we entered ; he was Supplied with refreshments when we got inside. Cress. examined by Mr. refreshments, would not swear there were nine persons on the premises, I did not count them. You have given them pretty good lati- tude. I had not seen Etches before he came out of Victoria-street, but I heard him coming up Victoria street. When he came into the Market-place, my at- tention was called to him. I could tell him by his brawling noise when in that state. He had seen two gentlemen in court who were in the hotel. They were there, it was nbt the first thne that he had seen them

there. Mr. Stead.—You mean to imply something about them. Witness.—l can do. Mr. Stead.—l have no doubt of your powers, you can do anything. It is very wrong for an officer to Imply anything of the kind. Mr. Harris.—You asked him. Witness.—Etches fell once against the wall, and up the steps against the door. He had the water bottle in his hand when witness went in. Mr. Ste ad.—That is what you say.. • Witness.—And that is what I maintain. Ur. Stead.—Of course. Do you consider it consis- tent with your duty as a police constable, finding a man—accorciing to your own statement—so drunk as this man, and making a noise in Victoria-street, to permit such a man to enter a beer-house or public- house I' Witness.-1 have nothing to do with it, or the con- ducting of his own house, he is the holder of the license. Mr. Stead.—However drunk a man who was going to a licensed house P Witness: I should not prevent him, and I should not - go in and tell the licensee. He was told by_ Herring- ton. When Etches came staggering up Harrington first spcke to him about being drunk. 'Witness said, "You ought to be ashamed of yeurself being drunk, a man in yourposition." Etehes had some conversation with Harrington and he gave him a shilling which he returned, which, fell on the floor, and in stooping to pick it up he reeled and fell against Youlton's shop. Witness smelt his breath which was very strong. r.o. Harrington stated that he was conversing at the top of Victoria-street with Constable Harvey when Etches came up. He was very drunk and commenced talking to witness, and said he, witness, was not a bad kind of chap, and put a shilling in his hand. Witness handed it back and said he would have it some other time. The shilling fell to the ground, and when I Etches was picking it up he staggered and would have fallen to the ground bad he not fallen against Youl- ton's shop. Witness advised him to go home in a friendly way, when he declined, and said that he was going to get a glass of whisky. Witness said "It's time all decent men were in bed, lam going part of your road." He refused to go home, and said he would go across and have a glass of whisky. When he started to go he would have fallen had he not em- braced a latepoet at the corner of V ictorta.street. Etches went staggering to the hotel and mounted the steps with difficulty. They heard him say "I'm as drunk as h—." They went in and saw him sitting by the fire place, with a glass of what he thought was Bruits before him. He had a bottle or something in his baud. The defendant said that he was not drunk or he must have seen him coming in. Witness said to Mr. Harvey, "I'm very sorry you have committed your- elf," he said "What P" and witness did not answer because the sergeant spoke to him. In reply to the Chairman witness said that haying known Etches for years he knew he was drunk. Cross-examined.—He distinctly heard the prisoner kay id rue as drunk as b.--." He never replied to the charge when he said he was drunk. He was cer- tain that that was the expression. The expression was !pot "as drunk as a fool," but "as drunk as Its was nearer than the sergeant. Mr. Stead, before calling the evidence for the de- fence, said that Mr. Harvey, the defendant, was of course well known in that court. He had for years conducted the 'Unicorn Hotel with satisfaction to the justices, and without conviction. le charge had ever r been made against Mr. Harvey or his mode of conduct- ing his house. There was nothing more evolting pinionoitess. his own ideas, than that of permitting dmiikeni1 in Be thought that whatever might be the o Bench with reference to the state of the man outettig the house, after they heard the evidence for the de_ fence, they would come to the conclusion that theie was no foundation whatever for that serious charge. It might, according to the evidence of witnesses, although he thought they would find a very important conflict of testimony.—lt might, for the purposes of the ease that day, be admitted that he might have been in a' etate ot drunkenness and demeaned himself as such outside, but demeaned himself as a sober man inside, and Mr. Harvey would have no reasonable grounds to suppose that the man was drunk, that charge must fall to the ground. The Licensing Act had received an interpretation from the superior courts with respect to gaming, and the Queen's Bench held that it was not sufficient to prove the fact of gaming, but there must e actual or constructive knowledge on the part of the person charged with permitting gaming. That he took it was similar in principle, and that it was not suffi- cient to prove permit:ing drunkenness without such a knowledge on the part of the licensee or his servants. Be would show them, from the evidence of Mr. Har- vey, Miss Banks, the barmaid, and gentlemen who wore in the bar, that Etches demeaned himself as a sober man, and that there was no foundation what- ever for such objectionable statements as those re- ferred to by the two officers, to say nothing about the difference as to what words were actually used. He asked the bench to consider fez a moment teee eitef4l 11501 W 911,14 IturlPl;apply

drink to a man who, according to the statement of the police officer, had paid be wa " As' drunk as and the other "As drunk at ab— feel." That at' once showed the improbability of the statement, and how far the polioe.were trying to fix upori Mr. Har- vey this charge—a charge from which- his nature would have revolted. There was another feature in the case which he bad never met with withoat it re- ceiving censure at the hands of the bench, and if lie were the person who had to deal with the evidence of witnesses who came into the witness box and said, "I saw that man staggering drunk, reeling, embracing a lamp post.; he had fallen two or three times:; I stood on the opposite side of the street and watched him in.; I gave him time to get his drink, ,and then appeared on the scene to complete against him the charge of permit- ting drankenness.Flf (said Mr. Stead) I know anything about the duties of the police, they are of a preventive character, and Harvey (the defendant) has as much right to their protection as anyone else. It was their duty to stop that man, or warn the servants of Mr. Harvey, if he was in the state they spoke of. Such conduct never passed before any bench of justices without receiving some censure on the part of the bench hearing such a case as that. It was the duty of the police to prevent drunkenness, and when, as they stated, Etches was in a beastly state of intoxication they allowed him to get another glass, although pre- viouely they had heard him making a disturbance on the highway. Why did they not arrest him, and take him to the lock.up if their case was true P The police were as much the custo:liens of the interest of the licensee as they were of the general public.' After hearing the evidence of Mr. Harvey, the barmaid, and Mr. Riley, the court would consider that the defen- dant had no grounds for supposing Etches was in a state of drunkenness, and that he demeaned himself as such when he came in and applied for liquor. He (Mr. Stead) for the purpose of his case need not dis- cuss whether the man was drunk or sober, .and the innkeeper was only responsible if he had reasonable grounds to suppose that he was drunk, or was satisfied that he was actually drunk. There was nothing which would justify the defendant or his servants in refusing to serve Etches. To the statement with regard to the objectionable language he should give the most complete denial. He should ask them (the Bench) as men of the world—and holding the law—who had to decide an important ease against a respectable innkeeper who had so long carried on his business without conviction, after they had heard the evidence for the defence to reject that evidence in toto, as an entire fabrication, and one he did not hesitate to say, which had been manufactured on the part of the police to bolster up the knowledge against the innkeeper. If the court had the slightest doubt about the matter he would ask them to adjourn the case in order that some gentlemen, out of town on business, could attend and give evidence before the court. The defendant, james Harvey, was sworn, he stated that he had kept the Unicorn Hotel ten years. On the night in question he had just come but of his room —in which he had been having supper—into the bar, where there were sitting Mr. Riley, Mr, Miller, Mr. Biradburn, and other gentlemen, who were engaged in business at Manchester. When Mr. Etches went. ,across the bar there was not the slightest indication of drunkenness. He, witness, gave up his seat to him, took his watch out, and said "Now, Etches, if you ' want a glass it's five minutes to ten, you had better be quick about it." Witness was standing by the door when Sergeant Harvey came in and said "You have got a man drunk here." Witness said "I'm not aware of it." He pointed out Mr. Etches, who, when he went out walked across the Market Place as sound as possible. He was in the bar when he came in, and that was the first time he or the other witnesses had heard anything of the expression "as drunk as a fool." Had any such expression been used he would not have forgotten it, and would not have supplied any man with drink, who introduced himself with such a state- ment as that. .

By Mr. Harris: Witness mustahave heard it, if such an expression had been made use of. By Superintendent Aston: There were nine persons in the bar at most, and such an expression could not have been used. Mr. Stead.—lt was heard outside, yet Mrs. Harvey came into the barland said "Are they all gone, they are so quiet P" Witness.—Whengliarvey charged' Etches he maid I'm not drunk." Miss Elizabeth Banks, barmaid at the Unicorn Hotel, stated that when Etches came in he never once reeled. She saw him enter at the door and come up the lobby. She corroborated the statement of Mr. Harvey, and stated that Mr. Etches was in the act of drinking when the policemen came in. There was not a water bottle on the table, she having removed them before they entered. Etches walked in quite straight, and walked out equally erect, and was apparently perfectly sober. Sue had had instructions from Mr. and Mrs. Harvey not to serve people of whose sobriety she had any doubt.- He dig not make use of any ex- pression, and only said "A glass of Scotch whisky." Amongst those in the bar, which was very quiet, were Mr. Riley, Mr. Bowen, and Mr. Mal em. Mr. Ben. Riley, saddler. Altrincham, who was in the hotel on the night in question, said that he knew Etches very well, and remembered his coming into the bar, and Mr. Harvey giving up his seat to him. He did not make use of the expression spoken of. He spoke to Etches, and went across the Market Piaci with him; he had had something to drink, but did not ail anything very much. He did not consider him. drunk, nor anything approaching drunkenness, If he had been going through the Market Place in the day time the poli ;e! would have taken no notice of him. By Mr. Harris.— Anyone could see that he had had a glass or two. It loosened his tongue a bit. He was talking quietly to witness. Thos. Miller, law student, stated that he was present, and saw Mr. Etches come in. He walked steadily, and sat down quietly and ordered something to drink, with which he was served by the barmaid. He passed wit- ness within half a yard. It was his impression— Mr. Harris.—You cannot give your impression. Mr. Stead.—No, that is only allowed on the part of the police. Witness.—l'll swear I saw him pour the water into his glass, and saw the baernaid take the bottle away, and directly after the police came in, when Etches had the glass iu his hand. There was nothing in the man's demeanour at the time that he was served with the liquor to lead him to suppose that he was an improper person to receive liquor. He did not say "Pm as drunk as h—," or anything of the kind. He did not show the slightest symptoms of intoxication in his walk, his appearance, or the way in which he gave his order. They went out together, and he asked Mr. Bowen to notice the man as he went across the road. He walked as steadily as you or I could do. Edward Bradburn, la* student, gave corroborative evidence, and stated that from the demeanour of the man when he crossed the bar, and at the time when he was served with liquor, there was nothing to lead the landlord or the barmaid to suppose that he was in a drunken state. He did not say, "I'm as drunk as h—" or anything to that effect. Witness was not four yards from him at any time. Mr. Stead stated that he couid not call Xr. Bowen, because he was out of town, and he would therefore leave the case in the hands of the court. The Chairman said that the bench were unanimously of opinion that Etches was drunk at the time. They had not only the clear and distinct language of the police, previous to enteriug the house, but that was in some measure confirmed by one of the witnesses for the defence, who said: he was ailing something. Etches would be fined 10s and Costs. As regarded Harvey, they believed that although Etches, when out of doors was drunk, and indicated it at the time, yet still he might have behaved himself for a few minutes in Mr. Harvey's house, and not shew.n any indications what- ever that he was under the influence of liquor. They should dismiss the ease against Mr. Harvey. With regard to the police, they had a most difficult and arduous duty to perform, and it would not have been wise for them to apprehend every man they conceived to be drunk, unless they, apprehended a breach of the peace. Mr. Stead said that his observations referred to their Preventingotateof ihntimox.icaHtieenthtoougghett pmeorrmeiltitqiungort,hie mnsteaandin a of Her Majesty's subjects were entitled to that. The Chairman.—How? Mr. Stead.—They could have prevented him, and that is the way to prevent drunkenness, if not the police are as much permitting drunkenness as the licensee is.
Mr. Aston.—l have not given them any such instruc. tions.
Mr. Stoad.—Then you ought to do.

APPRENTICESHIPS. LECTURE AT BOWDUN. •
The Rev. W. Cunningham delivered the fourth of a 6eries of lectures at Bowdon on Friday, the subject being" Apprenticeships, and the Relation of Capital to Labour."

The LECTIIABB, after dealing with the question of apprentioeshim said that it seemed to inui that if all special training- were discarded for special employ- ments ik would be the means of getting men who were Jacks of all trades and masters a none. At the same time,, though this special training was absolutely nedessary, MI it seemed to him, there might be a great deal of difference in regard to thd form which it ought to take. And this was what the dispute was generally about. There was, doubtless, still a great many evils in regard to the form whica this special training took, and that was the form of apprenticeship, for he thought this might be stated to be the case still, fon although in many of the trades that were rapidly developed, ap- prenticeships . were discarded for reasons it was not worth while to enter into, still in smaller trades they kept to the system of definitely binding a boy to a trade for a given number of years, and there were really obvious evils in regard to the boys and in regard to the masters. - They might hieve a boy tolerably clever who picked up his trade very easily, and came to do the work of a man, and then he had to work for the last two or three years of his time for extremely inadequate remuneration. That seemed to be an injustice to the boy. Again, they might have a boy who was absolutely idle and would not learn at all, and the master might have a great deal of difficulty in getting rid of him. These were the forms which the objections generally took; but in spite of all these difficulties it seemed very hard to substitute anything better. There , were various proposals made for special training by means of tech- meal schools, bet it was doubtful how far the work might be learnt prentically,and thoroughly in any sort of a achool, and a great deal which was said by People about t?chnical sohools being substituted for apprenticeship was really nonsense. People said that apprentices were very idle, and did not make use of their opportunities, and therefore instead of appren- ticeships they, ought to have schools, as if people never heard of boys being idle at school! The arguments would apply just as much against any other system that could be devised, so that it was not the system that was so much in fault as human nature. So that granting all these evils which were in connection with the apprenticeship system, granting that it did after all give a very inadequate test of a boy's having learnt his trade thoroughly and well, when be had been apprenticed to it for a certain length of time, with all its defects it seemed to him to be the best thing that could be devised at present, especially if some slight modifloations ,could be introduced. It was said that the apprenticeship system was a tedious and expensive process, that by the apprenticeship system a good many men were shut out, and so wages are raised and commodities are dearer than they otherwise would be. This was perhaps the case to some extent, and it was perhaps an evil to some extent, but he was net altogether sure. because it seemed to him to be far more important to have some attempt at a guarantee that the things they bought were made by skilful people, and fairly well made. In the present age there was great difficulty in regard to judging artiel-s that were offered for sale, simply because there was over com- petition, and a tendency to scamp work, and adultera- tion in every possible way, and any little thing that did render it probable that the work was done by tolerably skilled instead of un,killed men was advan- tageous. There had been times when a trade had been ruined, temporarily at all events, by a large introduction of unskilled workers. This was the case with the glass trade some years ago. The trade was flooded with apprentices,—that was to say, the work which ought to have been done by those who had learnt their trade was done principally by those who were learning, and therefore it was done extremely badly, and it had serious results in all sorts of ways. Having demonstrated that these things could not be brought about unless they had got a good deal of material wealth to start with, he said that a country could not get on unless it had got both a town and country population. It could not get on very fast unless it had a certain number who were labouriug with their hands and a certain number labouring with their heads.

div.head: AN ALTRINCHAM POLICEMAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT.
div.p: AN ALTRINCHAM POLICEMAN CHARGED WITH ASSAULT.

At the Altrincham Police ()curt, on Monday, acting Sergeant Harvey, was charged with assaulting David Barber, contractor, Lloyd-street, Altrincham, on the 23rd ult. The defendant pleaded not guilty. The complainant stated that on Monday, the 23rd Oct., he was at that court. He was standing on the first land- ing near the door, with his back against the iron rail- ings, when the defendant mune and called out "silence." A. woman named Butter smiled at him, and he went and called her a foul name—a grinning old devil, and took her by the shoulders and pulled her down to the bottom of the steps. Witness said "That woman has not spoken, and never opened her mouth." He came to him, got hold of him by the collar with one hand and the waist with the other, said "You b— old fool, you have been put out of court once— go down." He pushed him down to the bottom, and had he not stack to the Wilily:ha wouldhave gone over. -Ho-tola him he should report him for it. When he got to the bottom the-defendant said, "You old devil, go off these premises; if Ton come in here again I'll lock you up." By pressing him against the rails the defendand hurt complainant's side. Cross-examined Was quite certain as to the words used. He had not previously been requested to make a less noise and go away. There was a noise, but it was caused by the police at the bottom of the steps. Complain- ant admitted that .he had been summoned on one or two occasions, and bound over to keep the peace. He was sure the clef en- dent was the one who made use of the expression.— Cross-examination continued: He had summoned a party to that court and was bound over, the result being against the evidence. He had been fined 203. and costs for an assault on a man named Jenkinson, and had been summoned at other times before the court. He came to the police station the same night, and spoke to Superintendent Aston.—Thos.Bate, gardener, Islington-street, corroborated the statement of Mr. Barber. The Chairman.—Thea what was he to dol3 Richard Jenkinson, gardener, Timperley, also gave similar evidence, and stated further that the defendant called the woman who sat on the steps (Mrs. Rutter) an "old witch," and said to complainant "hold your noise you damned old fool. Cross-examined—Witness had been fined several times for assaults. Mrs. Sarah Barker, gave the same evi- dence, and further stated that she heard him say, " I have locked up many a better man than him, and if he comes on the premises again I'll lock him up." Mrs. Mary Rutter gave corroborative testimony, and stated that having been standing a long while, she sat down on the steps. The defendant came to the door, and said " you must make a less noise." She was not speaking to anyone and remarked, "women have nothing else to defend themselves with but their tongue' —(laughter) —meaning it as a joke. She then described being pushed down the steps, and the officer saying that if she spoke another word he would lock her up. Cross-examined—She did not say "now you people make a less noise, here's that long bobby." Defendant said he was on duty in the police court last Monday, and several times during the day Mr. Nichol- son, solicitor, complained of the great nom. He went to the door and complainant was then conversing with four or five women. He called out silence and came into court. In a short time afterwards Mr. Nicholson again complained, and he then went out with P.C. Newne, and told them that such a noise :could not be allowed any longer, and that they must go away. Two or three went away, but the complainant and the woman Rutter remained. She made a remark about women's tongues, and told them that the "long bobby" Was coming, and they must look out. He told them they had better go down as tney had monopolised the time of the court long enough, and as he was going past Barber he said that he (acting Sergeant Harvey) had made more noise than any of them. He turned round and said, "Go, or I'll remove you." He placed his hand on the muscle of his arm, told him again to go, and he went down chattering. He then told him to let him have none of his blackguardism, and Barber went away swearing what he had done for a better man, and that he would turn him out without a stripe to swagger with. He continued his noise outside, and he (defendant) returned into court. This was all the assault, and as to the bad language he thought more about this than the alleged assault. There was not a man in this or the adjoining county who could saythat be had heard him directly make use of a bad word, and he should call evidence on this point. P.C. Newns, stated that complainant was very in- solent, • and defendant merely took hold of him by the hand and put him down the steps. P.C. Beaney gave corroborative evidence, and said that complainant said, "It's you b— inside that have been kicking up the row, not us. I have to pay to keep such b— as You." We shall dismiss the case. Supt. Aston was sworn, and he stated that he had ex- pressed his surprise at such expressions being attribu- ted to the defendant, as he had never heard him use a bad word since he had been with him. The complan- ant complained to him, but said that he should not take any notice of it. The Chairman said that advo- cates had frequently complained of noise in court, and certainly such noise and interruption could not be allowed. They agreed with Mr. Aston that there was nothing so essential for a police officer as to be guarded In the language he used, and they believed that the defendant never made use of the language imputed to him, and acquitted him of it. div.head: ALTRINCHAM AND AID TO THE SERVIANS.
div.p: ALTRINCHAM AND AID TO THE SERVIANS.

The following letter, dated Hotel Krone, Belgrade, October 24, has been received from Dr. Ziemann, by the treasurer of the Manchester Evangelization Com- mittee, Mr. Wm. MiMe .—" If you had seen me last evening till long after midnight trying to sum up my accounts, even your stern treasurer's soul would have taken pity upon me. After all I could not do it, and Will ask to-day our consul to find some one to do it for me for payment. All I know is that I have spent £BO5 odd, including my own £6O, and also £l9 from my pocket. From your latest telegram I learn that I have again £6OO to spend. I had thoughts of coming home, but now I shall start cheerfully again to work. No description of mine could give you a comprehen- sive idea of what misery exists here. One must see it to believe it. In the grim, bitter cold days and nights which we have, accompanied, sometimes for days together, by pouring rain, there are still to my knowledge, in the district I personally visit, more than 20,000 people without shelter, and most of them clothed in what they wore during the hot summer months, and dependent fOr their daily food upon the morsel any charitable hand may chance to give them. On receipt of your telegram I ordered at once three more barracks, and I have written to my architect to build them if possible for from 3,000 to 4,000 persons. The Minister of the Interior sent me this morning a message that the Government will give me leave to take the timber from the forest without charge for my building purposes. This will save a great deal of money. I will spend £2OO in buying sheep• skin jackets. Dr. 6andwith has done the same, and tells me it is the most profitable outlay of money. With the rest of the money I will arrange for each district soup kitchens, so that at least the little ones and the weakest may have sometimes a little warm nourishment. Let me say here, once for all, that all the white linen things, such as shirts, pillow Cans, and sheets, are at present of little use here. They may be when the people are once again settled in their homes, but the great point for the moment is to protect them from the wet and cold. They wear here the coarsest material you can imagine. In fact, evdry bit of the wrappers of your goods has been thankfully accepted, and made up into shirts. Thick flannel and blankets are the only things I care to get from England. If you could only send them quickly, I would suggest that you should communicate with the different railway companies, and ask them for charity's sake to send the goods you forward by passenger trains at reduced fares. Then appeal through the Times, Daily .News, and other papers, to different manufacturers for at least 10,000 rough, thick blankets. They would be a real life-saving means here. I have been told that by way of Ham- burg. through Elkan and Co., goods would be quickest transported. I wish you would also move in the matter of the Orphan Home. All preliminaries are now settled. The Archbishop and the Government gave yesterday their distinct Rermission. Our consul, Mr. White, is willing to be the treasurer, and Mrs. White the responsible secretary. All that remains now is to place £3,000 as a fund in the hands of Mr. White. 117 orphans are waiting to be cared for. Can't you appeal to the Mansion House and the differ- ent committees for the relief of the Bulgarians Most of these orphans are Bulgarians. What better use could be made of the money than for such a purpose 1' I hear this week that hard fighting is going on, but Belgrade is the last place in the world to hear reliable news.

Much Christian love t 3 all friends, and espe- cially give my most warm thanks to your brave women in Altrincham.. Tell them their gifts of real sacrificing love have touched me greatly, and many people hero to whom I read your account were moved to tears. It may be something for them to hear that the Servian papers have taken notice of it with great praise, but it is more that it will not be for- gotten by the Judge of the earth when all our deeds will be summed up.—Yours, H. P. ZIEMAN N. •

div.head: MANUFAOTURE OF SODA
div.p: THE MANUFAOTURE OF SODA
FROM SALT.

At a meeting of the Manchester Scientific Students' Society, held a few evenings since at the rooms of the Literary and Philosophical Society, a lec- ture on the manufacture of soda from salt was given by the Ray. J. Preeston.

The Lstorrausis gave a description of salt, and of the instances and localities where it has ,been found to be naturally ,and abundantly deposited. Taking a section of the strata in one part of Cheshire, he pointed out the thickness and order of a number of beds of marls and sandstones, between which occurred layers of rock salt. Mr. Ward, of Winwick, had given it as his view of the origin of salt deposits, that . they were the result of the sea water evaporation in areas sur- rounded by hills except on one side opening to the sea, time and changes of level allowing the deposit of suc- cessive layers of salt, sand, and marl. The Lecturer himself was not content with any explanation of the origin of salt which he had yet met with in works on Geology, but he had no theory of his own to submit on .the subject. Re then described the discovery of chlorine in rock salt by Meek in 1774, and of the establishment of its elementary nature by Davy in 1810. Its properties were shown in experiments. The metal sodium was next described, and its discovery by Duhamel in 1736, by Marggraf in 1758, and Davy in 1807. . The latter first obtained the metal from salt. Its curious properties were shown by experiments. The processes of making soda, invented by Lehlane in 1870, and subsequently perfected by other chemi,ts, were shown to consist of three site ges The conversion of chloride of sodium into a sulphate by sulphuric acid ; the conversion of this sulphate into carbonate with a limestone; and the lixiviation of the soda in hot water. The lecturer was assisted in his descriptions by show- ing plans of the construction of the apparatus for soda manufacture in a large works. The stages of chang- ing salt into salt cake, black balls, or crude •soda, soda ash, and crystal soda were explained in detail. The various contrivances for preventing the emission o! dense volumes of noxious vapours from alkali works were also described, and the lecturer spoke strongly , against the carelessness of the owners of works in this respect. Dr. Roscoe had shown that 95 per cent of these deleterious gases could be caught and retained, and that the chimneys of such works could be made to emit comparatively pure air and steam. The bye-pro- ducts from the manufacture of soda were also described, and their respective values shown in various ways.

A discussion followed, in which the Chairman, Mr. Stirrup, M. Horsfall, and Mr. Rogers took part, their remarks being directed to the cost of making soda by this process; the natural deposits of salt and of soda in Egypt. Peru, and Hungary; and the oiled of the gases in destroying vegetation,—Afanoltaster Citv News.

div.head: POPULAR LECTURES AT NORTH-
div.p: POPULAR LECTURES AT NORTH-
WIOH.

The second lecture of the series was delivered in the Drill Hall, en Thursday evening, by Mr. T. Ward on ",Language." The chair was occupied thy the Rev. J., F. Rountlawaite. The lecturer said that language was the means by which men conveyed the thoughts and impressions of their minds to other :men. This might be done to some extent by signs which were the most natural and perhaps the first means of communication. As however from the nature of things it was quite im- possible to convey complicated iimpressions in this way men soon zetiorted to sound, being possessed of an in- strument—the tongue—which was capable of express- ing a large number of sounds, the combinations of which formed sufficient variety to express all thoughts. As sound was only capable of use at limited distances and when the speaker was present, when distant communications became necessary, or permanent re- cords of sayings desired, pictures were made, convey- ing to the eye the idea desirous of being impressed. The picture fell as far short of being able to express co eiplicated ideas as. the signs and gestures, so that in process of time certain pictures were understood to re- present certain sounds and thus a hieroglyphic or pic- ture alphabet came into use. For simplicity's sake the figure soon took a simpler form and certain characters represented certain sounds, and thus arose the alphabet. Some of the most expressive language was that of gestures. Semaphores, railway signals, coloured lights, telegraphic signs, picture stories in children's book, Bsc., all showed that vivid impressions could be conveyed by similar means to those used in the first infancy of mankind. The human voice all the world overwaenearly the same, and capable of pro- ducing in conjunction with the tongue, teeth, lips, palate, and throat, the same sJunds, And all the tan. guage of the world contained no more than some GO distinct sounds. The lecturer said the stud yof lan- guage, as distinguished from the learning of a language was extremely interesting and fascinating, and he could not recommend any one to undertake a more delightful task than to follow up what he had but sketched in outline. The Chairman announced that the next lecture would be delivered by Mr, Grossinith, that day fortnight, and the chair would be taken by an old friend, Mr. E. Leader Williams.

DEATH OF AN OLD MUSICAL CONDUCTOR. It is with sincere regret we announce the death of Mr. Councillor Oakden, which took place at his resi- dence, Stockton Mount, on Wednesday morning last, after a somewhat protracted and painful illness. The deceased gentleman was born at Bollington, near Macclesfield, on September 2nd, 1821, and has conse- quently just completed his 62nd year. His taste for the' musical profession seems to have been inherent, for when 18 years old he joined the band of the Ist Royal Diagoon Guards, of which regiment his father was bandmaster. Subsequently he succeeded him in that capacity, and held his appointment for a number of years, twelve of which he spent with the regiment in Ireland. Mr. Oakden, sen , was appointed bandmaster to the 4th Royal Lancashire Militia, whose head- quarters were at Warrington. In this position he was a les succeeded by his son, who accepted the appoint- ment upon leaving the Dragoon Guards, and for 18 years the deceased gentleman discharged his duti...l with credit and ability, and in such a manner as to win the estee al of both his brother officers and his sub w- dinates. Mr. Oakden was a musician of no mean order. On account of his musical capacity, which was gener- ally admitted throughouthis profession, he was chosen, when the regiment was at Aldershot, musical director to the brigade, during a grand review held before the Queen, and so successful was the musical performances of the combined bands under Mr. Oakden's leader- ship that he received through General Knollys her Majesty's warm expression of appreciation of his musical services. Upon taking up his residence in War- rington, Mr. Oakden devoted himself with consider- able energy to the cultivation of music in the town, and his own progress, together with the many high-class concerts given by him, are well remembered testimo- nills of his success. Wartingtonians have been well favoured with opportunities of listening to the best artistes in the musical world, and his efforts in this direction have not lacked substantial appreciation. For several years he served as a member of the Board of Guardians, and also as a town councillar, and in each capacity earned the respect, of his colleagues. In their bereavement his widow and family will receive the cordial sympathy of their friends and neighbours,

div.head: MYSTERIOUS MURDER.
div.p: MYSTERIOUS MURDER.

A coroner's jury held at Manchester returned a Me dict of wilful murder in the case of Winifred Mark. rand, aged 27, who was found dead in bed under mysterious circumstances on the 4th inst. An analysis of the contents of the stomach of the deceased showed that death bad been caused by chloroform, ble the jury found that there was no evidence to show by whom it had been administered. Father Daly, of Storkroit who has charge of is Roman Catholic chapel at Runcorn, having been referred to by some of the witnesses, the reverend gentleman asked the coroner if he thought there was any evidence against him. The coroner said there was indirect evidence that he (F ether Daly) was the last person seen going into the house of the deceased, at ten o'clock at night; and subsequently, in summing up the evidence to the jury, the coroner said the poison was probably taken into the house of the deceassd by the person who called at ten o'clock. Father Daly avowed his entire innocence of any improper connection with the deceased, and called witnesses to show that he was at Runcorn be. tween nine and WI o'clock on the night in question. THE ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A RUNCORN PRIEST.

Little sympathy exists in Runcorn with the rumour: which have mixed up Father Daly's name with the mysterious affair at Manchester. Public feeling in the town where Father Daly resides is entirely in his favour. The tßuncorn police can testify that on the night of the alleged murder he was talking to some of the members of the force at the police office door at twenty minutes to ten, the very time he was said to have entered the house. He has resided in Runcorn three months, and during that time he has not only gained the ecteem of his flock, but also oft -e Protestant clergy and the inhabitants of the town. His services on Sunday were Et:ended by crowded congregations, and his friends who are conversant with the whole airair state that his dealings with the unfortunate woman were totally those of a philanthropic character and it was with a view to reclaim her from the erring life which she had adoptod that he visited her house. However, in Runcorn itself not the slightest importance is attached to the allegations which have been made.

div.head: SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 4, 1876.
div.p: SATURDAY. NOVEMBER 4, 1876.
SIR GILBERT GREENALL AT POMONA GARDENS.

TEE Conservative carnival, or gala, or de- monstration, or whichever is the most correct title, held in Manchester last week, ter- minated on Saturday at the Pomona Gardens. Perhaps carnival is the most correct designation of the brawl. Italian carnivals are held just before Lent: it is the period of sanctioned licence which precedes the perici of compulsory fasting and peni- tence; and in this respect the Tories of Lancashire have unconsciously followed the precedent of Rome. They have danced and feasted, they have jested with the national honour, and cut capers with the national exchequer, and assuredly their Lent is at hand, when they shall, 89 before, not during forty days, but during forty years, do political penance, and renounce the emolu- ments and the patronage of office. But while their carnival lasts, we must not grudge them the gaiety for which they will have to pay with grief. As a matter of humanity, we should not remind them, in the hour of intoxication, of the inevitable hour of dejection which must follow. So far from this, we propose decorously to enter the carouse, to mingle with the revellers, and to pay a flying visit to Pomona Gardens— that shrine dedicated to horse and cattle shows, and Conservative demonstrations. The programme of Saturday's sports was simply magnificent, platform and pit accom- modation were provided for untold thou- sands, and if only the people had come and paid their money like honest Conservative working men, the closing scene of the car- nival would, like the setting sun, have eclipsed in size and splendour its eastern self. But unfortunately the Conservative working men did not arrive, with their six- pences, in sufficient numbers to fill the place, and what might have been a glorious meeting in the Public Hall of Warrington, was a thin and shabby meeting in the dancing saloons of Pomona. Yet, in an- ticipation of a stupendous gathering, it was arranged to hold both an " importint " meeting in the casino and a " subsidiary " meeting in the stables, and it must have been a question of considerable delicacy on the part of the master of the ceremonies to decide who was important and who was sub- sidiary. It is with undisguised surprise and the bitterest jealousy that we read that Sir Gilbert Greenall, Baronet, was shown into the stable, where, in spite of the fact that the floor was thickly carpeted with sawdust, and that thus the trampling of Conservative bluchers was inaudible, we are informed that he spoke so " feebly " that he is scarcely reported. In what sense the word "feebly" is used we do not know. We can only assure our readers that Sir Gilbert is in ex- cellent health. In the large hall, the usual delay and dispiriting banter occupied the audience before the talking began. Cheers called for Lords Derby and Beaconsfield, even when their i'dll-length portraits were exhibited, pasted on Sunday school banners, could not be said to be enthusiastically re- sponded to; while Messrs. Peter Rylands and Jacob Bright were only honoured with half-hearted groans. Indeed, it seams that the only episodes which really fired the enthusiasm of the meeting were the occa- sional advent of glittering banners and deafening brass bands • and this being dis- covered by the public men who had to ascend the platform, it was ingeniously con- trived that they entered the meeting in small detachments, simultaneously with a brass baud, and then by raising their hate at the right moment, and bowing in acknow- ledgment of the cheers, who could say that they did not receive a cordial reception? But the second meeting, at which Sir Gilbert Greenall, Baroaet, moved the first resolution, was not even enlivened by brass bands, but, as if they had been enter- tained to the flat dregs of the wine, their pleasure was destroyed by the sound of the music from the saloon, loud enough to drown the the voices partially, but, unfortunately, not entirely. We need hardly say that we take our report of Sir Gilbert's speech from the Tory Manchester Courier, for it is the only newspaper which gives us an intelligible account, and it is a remarkable fact, and one highly creditable to the reporter of that paper, that he heard every word that our member uttered, while the representatives of the Manchester Guardian and of the Examiner heard little, and understood less. Gilbert was entrusted with the follow- ing resal,u.tion :—" That this meeting ex- presses the iilill!lst confidence in Her Majesty's present Governnt. and its high admiration of the wisdom and statesrii..?.nlike ability it has shown in the conduct of publie affairs. It further desires to record its un- qualified approval of the foreign policy of the Administration, especially in relation to the i, astern question, believing that that policy has restored the prestige of England, maintained the honour and integrity of the empire, and been prompt€ d by a regard for the best interests of humanity.' In moving it, he said that it was an admirable thing to have a heart to be able to say that we have, at the head of the Government of this day, a body of "noblemen and gentlemen" in whom we have all the fullest confidence. There is an unpleasant ring about the words "noblemen and gentlemen." They suggest too much a brewer's circular appealing to the "noblemen, gentry, and clergy" of the district to purchase his beer. But this is only f . sentimental reflection, by the way, and perhaps, in high life, people do make a distinction between baronets and gentlemen. We have, before now, had occasion to (a- pnea our belief that Sir Gilbert enjoys the full confidence of his leaders, and that they repose in him the gravest secrets of the State, and our conviction is strengthened by his authoritive utterance of Saturday last. He tells usthat "the Government of the pre- sent day did not obtain its high distinction by any party practice or political trick." Now, it cannot be denied that it has hitherto been popularly - believed that Lord Beaconsfield has always succeeded by trickery and dubious political leg rdemain, and not by honest and single-minded aims. But when a man of Sir Gilbert's authority as a politician and his rank in life are con- sidered, we can no longer refuse to doubt that, in his own words "true Conservatism is as open as the sky" and a great deal more to this effect. With regard to the Eastern question, Sir Gilbert was naturally reticent, considering his relations with the cabinet, but he expressed it as his own private Opinion, that in this matter the present Government has been "constitutional, op eil, liberal, and honest." This is reassuring in the face of the repeated charges that it has been unconstitutional, deceitful, narrow, and disingenuous, and will no doubt have an effect upon the country. At least it might have had, had it not been for those abomin- able brass bands which prevented the repre- sentatives of the two journals, which have influence and a large circulation, from hear- ing the speech, and doomed poor Sir Gilbert to be buried alive in the dreary political grave, which the Manchester Courier is - ”-hitigoltc(ll/ cliggixg Or 014

MR. ASHWORTH AND THE COMMERCIAL CRISIS,

THE quarterly meeting of the Manchester Chamber of Commerce held on Monday last was more than usually interesting. The "dismal science" is it may be "caviare to the general" but it has its attractions, and what is more, its laws are inexorable, and must be followed and obeyed, or they will consume those wao disregard them. The speeches of Mr. Edmund Ashworth, President of the Chamber, and Mr. Jacob Bright, M.P., are well worthy the attention of masters and operatives at a great crisis like the pre- sent. Both of these gentlemen have, with their families and forefathers, been long identified with the manufacturing and industrial interests of this country. From the words of these gentlemen it may be gathered that the selfishness and distrust of nations is the curse of trade and com- merce. In great crises and supreme moments of peoples, it is quite conceiveable and even patriotic that "ways and means" must be raised somehow. But it is in times of peace and commercial credit that the seeds of disorganization and panic are sown, and woe betide those who disregard the first elements of eommercial probity, and wisdom, and truth in the early beginnings, and "piping times of peace." Mr. Ashworth gave some valuable and trustworthy statis- tics regarding our relative transactions wi,h Itussia and Turkey. Mr. Ashworth pointed out that at the present time the bullion in the various banks of Europe was largely in excess of all previous years within the memory of most men. In the Bank of France there are at present £83,800,000 sterling in bullion, in the Bank of Eng- land £33,194,000, in Germany £25,000,000, ia Austria £13,000,000, and in the Net,er- lands £12,967,000. Mr. Ashworth very shrewdly added that to attempt to govern the monetary fluctuations of the world was about as impossible a task as the governing of the waves of the sea. That is quite cor- rect,but at the same time weatherwise,scien- tific prophets, are able to tell us with remark- able exactness, which way the wind is likely to blow, and when and whence storms are to be expected. The enormous amount of bul- lion collected and held in reserve by the European Banks, certainly shows a paralysis of trade,but in that lie the hopes and safety of the future. It seems almost fool-hardy at a crisis and dislocation of affairs like the present, when diplomatists and governments are apparently at their wits enl, to say that there will be no European war, and yet that is our deliberate conviction. Our own Government has drifted from its original moorings, and it is as clear as noon-day that they do not intend to fight. Mr. Jacob Bright may be over sanguine and premature in his views as to the waters leading to the Black Sea being opened to the navies of the world, but it must be plain to every one after recent events that an attitude of distrust, de- fiance, and threat, is fatal to the peace and prosperity of the world. We can only echo Mr. Jacob Bright's words with regard to commercial difficulties nearer home, and say that in the ualortunate dispute which has arisen in North and North-East Lancashire, between masters and men, there will be found sufficiant wisdom to avoid the terrible crisis, which, without sense and forbearance is certain to come upon them.

A PUBLIC SPIRITED CONSERVATIVE.

The Town Council of Liverpool appears to be rapidly fallirg from the high position it once held in the estimation of its electors. The Daily Post as- acrts that "the deliberate pushing forward of drink men who have rendered the town no service is rapidly reducing the Corporation of Liverpool to the level of that of New York." The open alliance of the Conser- vatives with the beer interest has provoked a very de- ive protest from a well-known member cided and eff.let of the Conservative party. This gentleman' who was recently elected to the Select Vestry, allowed himself to be nominated for Scotland Ward without intending to go to the poll, in order to defeat the tactics of his own Ward Committee, who were de- sirous, he says, to adopt as their candidate 'a well-known monopolist brewer and ginshop owner' who was prepared to pay the shot, and might have gained the seat he desires had no other Conservative candidate been nominated." To prevent such a result Mr. Thomas came forward, and the Ward Committee thereupon "held itself back from the dis- graceful step for which it had made preparation." In other words, the brewer was not nominated; and Mr. Thomas, having gained his point, now reads his party a lesson by withdrawidg his name from the list of can- didates, and leaves the field clear for the Liberals. His farewell address to the discomfited Committee is ex- cellent. " I am one of those men," he says. " and there are many on my own side of politics, who will have no longer part or lot in conspiring to keep this great borough under the heel of drinksellers. There are jobbers enough in the Council looking out for corner lots without degrading the ward in which lam a large ratepayer by sending in another such represen- tative of selfish interest."

Military events, equally with the exigen- cies of diplomacy, seem to tend naturally to a very early solution of the Eastern diffi- culty. div.head: CHESTER.
div.p: CHESTER.

The only ward in Chester not contested this year was that of St. John's, consisting of 800 votes. With the exception of St. Os wald's ward, politics did not enter into the contest; but in that ward, which contains a large majority cf Liberals, it was decided to do away with the political absurdity of retaining Mr. Davies (who is the chairman of the Working Men's Conser,. vattve Association), and replace him with a good Liberal, Mr. Brown, who was returned by 780, against Davies 146.

div.head: SOUTHPORT.
div.p: SOUTHPORT.

There has beau no ward contests this year at South- port. Mr. Walter Smith, who has fulfilled the duties of mayor for the past two years, will be succeeded by Mr. Richard Nicholson, who, litre his predecessor in office, is a Liberal. Mr. Nicholson is a member of the Society of Friends.
A. MOTHER AND CHILD DROWNED IN THE MERSEY,

The wife of a gardener residing near Northenden, Cheshire, drowned herself and child, five years old, on Saturday last, in the river Mersey. The unhappy wretch had been drinking during the week, and quarrels with her husband ensuing, she chose this dismal way of escaping from her follies and her miseries.

div.head: FINES OF £3lO FOR BEING DRUNK.
div.p: FINES OF £3lO FOR BEING DRUNK.

On Tuesday, at the Marylebone Police Court, Ann Blades, 62 years' of age, was sentenced to 21 days' im- prisonment for being drunk and makin g use of bad language. The woman's husband, who stated that he had already paid £3lO 10e. in fines for her on account of similar c fiences, entreated the magistrate to impose a penalty, but the request was refused.

div.head: BALACLAVA HO AT NVAitaINGFON.
div.p: A BALACLAVA HO AT NVAitaINGFON.

Amongst the guests at the banquet to the Balaclava survivors, at the Westminster Palace this week, was Sergeant-major O'Dancghue, of Warrington, band. master of the 4th Royal Lancashire Miljta.lt.;,) was the veritable trumpeter who sounded he historical charge at Balaclava, where ht! served as trumpeter to the Bth Hussars. He tlso served in that capacity under Lord Cardigan in the campaign up the Danube and th:ough Bulgaria, three months before the Bala- clava engagement. When siding into the fatal encounter he was accompanied by his brother, but he returned from the fight alone, the fortune of war hav- ing robbed him of his brother's companionship. O'Donoghtie wears on his breast honours from France, Turkey, and England, and is a good specimen of what our soldiers were when England gained its martial prestige.

div.head: RAILWAY FROM WIGAN TO GLAZE. BROOK.
div.p: THE RAILWAY FROM WIGAN TO GLAZE. BROOK.

On Friday the Home Secretary cut the first sod of the Wigan Junction Railways, a line projected to pro- vide better transit for coal, and to connect Wigan with the Cheshire Lines at Glazebrook, and so with other great railway systems. Mr. Cross delivered a short address, in which he thanked the directors for the honour conferred upon him, and hoped the new rail- way would improve the state of affairs on some of the Lancashire lines. He was in favour of reducing labour by all means, for there was always some other field where it could be employed. The new railway would open out fresh coalfields, and so become both a benefit to the coalowners and the public. A luncheon was afterwards given, and presided over by Mr. Eskersley, chairman of the board of directors.

div.head: DISPUTED OWNERSHIP OF A DOG.
div.p: DISPUTED OWNERSHIP OF A DOG.

At the Warrington County Court, on Thursday, be- sore Mr. Wynne Ffoulkes, judge, and a special jury, David Green, draper, of Bridge-street, fined James Baines, a solicitor's clerk, a No. ,8, Bewsey-street, for L 5, being the value of a dog which belonged to the plaintiff, and which had been detained by the defend- ant. Mr. Nicholson was for the plaintiff, and from the evidence adduced it appeared that Mr. Green had a black retriever dog, and by some means or other it got into the possession of the defendant, who refused to give it up. An action was brought against him, and an order made for him to deliver up the dog and pay the costs. Before he did so, however, the animal died, and the present action was to recover its value. The defendant stated that it had been given to him by Mr. Potter, of the White Hart Hotel, about whose premises it had taken up its abode. From the evidence of Mr. Hayes it appeared the animal died from hydrophobia, having been bitten by a mad dog. The jury returned a verdict for the plaintiff, damages £l, with costs.

div.head: SWINDLER AT LYMM.
div.p: A SWINDLER AT LYMM.

During the past week Lymm has been visited by an audacious swindler. The man in question called at the house of a woman—whose generosity certainly over- stepped her discretion—and stated that he was em- ployed by the telegraph authorities, that he had come from London and wanted lodgings. He also represen- ted that he expected a " friend " for whom he wanted lodgings, but, fortunately for the victim of his roguery, her somewhat humble dwelling could not furnish ac- commodation for more than one peism, in addition to the members of her own family. After being provided with tea the man left the house with the ostensible purpose of inquiring at the post office for news of his 'friend," who was to bring him money. The news was forthcoming he said, but not the money, and as he had left his luggage at Warrington station, he was desirous of borrowing such a stun as would en. able him to fetch it. This plausible tale had the de. sired effect, and the man lett for Warrhigton, with a few shillings lent him by his oonlllag landlady. Neither the man nor his friend have since been heard of, and it will be fortunate for both of them, if they carefully avoid Lymm in the future, lest they find less eligible apartments than those they pretended to seek.

The Pope having desired to divide the Archbishoprio of Lyons into two dioceses at his own pleasure and without the assent of the French Government, the latter has issued a decree putting a stop to this beginn• ing of an encroachment on the part of the Vatican.
